Green Loom · Retail catalog

The product stayed the same. Everything around it changed.

A store can run out of stock, change a price, or need a new lab certificate without changing the product itself. As Green Loom’s co-founder, I designed a retail catalog that lets operators manage those changes without rebuilding the product.

Role
Co-founder
Scope
Retail catalog model and operator workflow
Key decision
Separate product identity from store operations and lab evidence
Outcome
Selected design direction, approved wireframe baseline, and a public schema

I — Inspiration

A product page wasn’t enough to run the catalog

The catalog needed to describe what a product was and help a store decide whether it could sell it. Those are different jobs. A product might have several packages, a different price at each store, and lab evidence that expires while its description stays the same.

Reviewing the operating workflow, CMS wireframes, and product definitions exposed the problem: facts with different sources and lifecycles were treated as product attributes. Potency appeared editable even though it came from a lab result. Store prices and quantities sat beside content shared across locations.

Georgia’s consumable-hemp rules made these distinctions consequential. Retail sale of hemp flower and leaves is prohibited. Products need a publicly available full-panel certificate of analysis, or COA, contracted within the last 12 months. Labels must provide the results or QR access to them.

Georgia Department of Agriculture retail guidance informed the product-form, evidence, and labeling requirements.

D — Design Process

Block the listing, not the product’s identity

I gave lab evidence its own record and validity period. When a certificate expires, the designed publication check blocks the affected store listing and tells the operator what needs attention. The product’s description and packages remain intact.

The recovery path is to review and link replacement evidence, then check the listing again. The operator fixes the fact that changed instead of recreating the product.

D — Design Process

Give each kind of change its own place

I separated the catalog into five records, so every update did not have to become a product edit:

  • Product holds the shared identity and content; Variant describes a sellable package.
  • Listing is a store’s offer; Inventory tracks that variant’s stock at the store.
  • Lab Result supplies testing evidence for the applicable product or variant.

Use the certificate as a source, not just an attachment

I designed the COA capture flow to turn lab evidence into traceable catalog data. An operator adds the certificate, reviews the extracted results, and links them to the applicable product or variant. Values such as potency stay connected to the lab result that supplied them.

E — Engagement

Use the wireframes to make the model concrete

The wireframes brought the model into everyday tasks: adding a package, preparing a store offer, checking evidence, and updating stock. I used the same vocabulary across the screens and publishing checks so each action had a clear home.

These explorations made the boundaries visible: lab evidence explains publication readiness, while a stock adjustment belongs to a specific variant and location.

A — Action

Guide the first publication. Speed up the next update.

We compared browsing by record type, a guided launchpad, and a queue of work spanning the catalog. I chose guided setup for the first publication, with direct catalog and inventory workspaces for returning operators.

Both paths use the same records; the guidance changes with the task:

  • First publication: add the product, review its evidence, and resolve readiness checks.
  • Stock update: find the item, adjust its stock, and review availability.

A — Action

Make the data portable without dictating the interface

Research into existing standards and vendor formats did not yield a complete product-data contract for this catalog. We developed and published the versioned Cannabis Product Schema. Its neutral core describes Product, Package, LabResult, Label, and Party. A Georgia hemp profile adds local constraints without embedding them in the core.

The Georgia profile applies product-form, testing, labeling, and potency constraints to that shared data.

The schema defines exchanged data; the retail application organizes the operator’s work. Keeping those responsibilities separate lets the interface support editing, publishing, and stock updates without being constrained by the shape of an import file.

S — Status and next steps

A working foundation for the catalog

The work produced a selected information architecture, an approved wireframe baseline, and a published Cannabis Product Schema. The next step is operator validation of the complete publication flow, including COA import and the checks that determine whether a listing is ready.

My design intent is to help operators see what changed, where to fix it, and what that means for the store’s offer. Operator testing still needs to establish whether those boundaries make the catalog easier to manage.
